title: Joining sentences, and making suggestions
goal: Break free of short sentences: join two ideas into one with -고, -지만 and -아서/어서, then invite others along with -(으)ㄹ까요.
bekal: wrapping up a conversation and saying goodbye properly

dialogs.title: 대화 — Planning the last day
dialogs.intro: The last unit. Notice that the sentences here are much longer than in unit one — not because the vocabulary is harder, but because the short sentences you've mastered are now joined into one.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Ani, if you have time tomorrow, shall we have lunch together?
lines.literal: Ani — Ms., tomorrow — time — exists-if — together — lunch — eat-shall-we?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Sure! I have class in the morning, but the afternoon is free.
lines.literal: good! morning-in — as-for — class — subject — exists-but — afternoon-in — as-for — fine.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Then shall we meet at one?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Yes. Let's eat and have coffee too.
lines.literal: yes. rice — object — eat-and — coffee — also — drink.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Sounds good. By the way, Ani, are you going back to Indonesia next week?
lines.literal: good. by-the-way, Ani — Ms., next — week-in — Indonesia-to — go?

lines.speaker: 아니:

lines.literal: yes. Korea — life — subject — really — good-because — go — want — not.

lines.speaker: 수지:

notes: **-고 links two actions without saying how they're related.** 밥을 먹**고** 커피를 마셔요 = eat and then have coffee. It simply strings them together, without saying one causes the other. It's the easiest connector of all: attach it straight to the stem, vowel or consonant.

**-지만 means "but" and also attaches straight to the stem.** 있**지만**, 좋**지만**, 먹**지만**. The only difference from 하지만 (which starts a new sentence) is position: -지만 joins two parts into one sentence, 하지만 splits them into two.

**-아서/어서 expresses a reason, and follows the same rules as the 해요 form.** 좋아요 → 좋**아서** (because it's good). 먹어요 → 먹**어서**. 공부해요 → 공부**해서**. ⚠️ The reason always comes **first** and the result after — whereas English often puts "because" second.

**⚠️ -아서/어서 can't take the past tense.** "Because it rained yesterday" is not 비가 왔어서 but 비가 **와서**. The past is marked only on the last verb of the sentence: 비가 와서 집에 있**었**어요. Almost every learner makes this mistake, and it's very noticeable.

**⚠️ -아서/어서 also can't be followed by a command or suggestion.** "Since it's raining, let's stay home" can't be 비가 와서 집에 있을까요. For that you use another connector, -(으)니까: 비가 **오니까** 집에 있을까요. The rule looks minor but is a favorite exam question.

**-(으)ㄹ까요? covers two intentions: suggesting and offering.** 같이 갈까요? = shall we go together? (a suggestion). 제가 할까요? = shall I do it? (an offer). Both are much softer than asking directly, because they leave the decision to the other person.

**덕분에 means "thanks to".** It's used for good things and almost always to say thank you. Its counterpart 때문에 ("because of") is neutral and often used for bad things. Swapping them can turn praise into a subtle accusation.
**-죠 is a shortened -지요, and it asks for agreement.** 그렇죠? = "right?". 당연하죠! = "of course!". This ending makes a sentence sound friendly and inviting, and it's everywhere in real conversation.

grammars.title: Three connectors that round off A1
body: All of them attach to the first verb, and tense is marked on the last verb of the sentence.

head: Connector
Meaning
How to attach
Example
rows: because (can be followed by a suggestion)

after: **-고 and -아서 can both mean "and then", and the difference is subtle but real.** 밥을 먹**고** 갔어요 = I ate, then left (two separate actions). 집에 가**서** 잤어요 = I went home and slept **there** (the second happens because of, or at the place of, the first). If the two actions are closely linked, -아서 is the right one.
**-(으)면 means "if" and is very common in polite requests:** 시간이 있으면 알려 주세요 ("if you have time, please let me know"). It softens whatever follows.

grammars.title: -(으)ㄹ까요? — suggesting and offering
body: The form is exactly like the -(으)ㄹ 거예요 and -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 you've already mastered: ㄹ for vowel stems, 을 for consonant stems.
after: **For a firmer suggestion there's -(으)ㅂ시다** (갑시다 — "let's go"), but ⚠️ this form is **impolite to older people**, even though it looks formal. With a boss or anyone older, stick to -(으)ㄹ까요? or simply the 해요 form: 같이 가요.
**The safest way to suggest something in any situation is the plain 해요 form with rising intonation:** 같이 가요? It's polite, never out of place, and it's what Koreans use most in everyday life.

blocks.title: 수고하셨습니다 — the phrase you'll hear most in Korea
items: Said at the end of a meeting, a class, a work shift, to the courier delivering a parcel, to anyone who has just finished something. It means roughly "thank you for your hard work".
⚠️ To someone older or a boss, this form can sound as if you're evaluating their work. With them, 감사합니다 is safer.
The everyday forms are 수고했어요 (to someone younger or the same age) and 수고하세요 (to someone who is still carrying on with their work).

blocks.text: Twenty units done. If you've worked through them seriously, you can now introduce yourself, point at things, count, tell the time, talk about yesterday, order food, go shopping, say what you want, decline politely, ask the way, and join all of it into flowing sentences. That's no small thing.
